item.title: Gábor Szabó – 1969
item.description:
Last week, Spotify bought WhoSampled. For those who do not know, it’s a massive community-driven database of information on reused music. Spotify says it will add WhoSampled’s data to the platform through a forthcoming “SongDNA” feature. The internet’s busiest music nerd, Anthony Fantano, is concerned about the purchase, most importantly because it might give major labels more power to earn money through credits.

The moments I enjoy samples the most are when I stumble upon the original and it turns out to be better— especially when the original is on an album full of beautiful songs. This happened when I heard Gábor Szabó’s “Stormy”, which you’ll instantly recognise from John Legend’s “Save Room”. Gábor himself is not afraid of reusing music either, as most of the songs on “1969” are covers. As can be read on WhoSampled.

item.title: Caribou – Honey
item.description:
I don’t think this is Caribou’s best album, and I didn’t listen to it for a while after hearing the first time. However, after seeing the man on Best Kept Secret this year, I was impressed how well the music works live. Last weekend, a friend gave me the record as a birthday present and I got to revisit it.

Something special happened when I reached the third track ‘Volume’. I got a beautiful flash back to Rainbow Disco Club festival in Japan last year, when Four Tet played it in the beginning of his set. This tune was a great start of a long night full of energy on the dance floor. The recording of Four Tet is on SoundCloud, check it out.

item.title: Todd Terje - It's Album Time
item.description: This album recommendation might be old for some. Others might only know the hit song ‘Inspector Norse’, which was very popular at parties over ten years ago. ‘It’s Album Time’ (2014) is one of those dance LP’s I often play entirely, as the songs smoothly transition into the next, and have a coherent Space Disco sound. Also, I get reminded of this album a lot when I hear similarities in other music. Like last weekend, at Parallel festival near Barcelona. Denato Dozzy played ‘Apex Break’ by Torn Hawk and Black Deer (2025), and the crazy arps immediately made me think of Terje’s ‘Preben Goes to Acapulco’. When I shared this reference with a friend, he agreed and showed me that in turn Terje’s track was based on ‘Solstice’ by Brian Bennet (1978). I guess we live in a postmodern remake culture, that just keeps on giving. Speaking of remakes, be sure to check out the original version of ‘Johnny and Mary’ by Robert Palmer, which is nicely covered by Bryan Ferry of Roxy Music on ‘It’s Album Time’.

item.title: Wilson Tanner - Legends
item.description: While writing this, I’m in that hazy state of happiness and tiredness, as it’s the Monday after three days of Best Kept Secret festival. I’m re-watching the concert registrations on my phone, while lying in sun. Little kids are jumping in the water next to my house, and I’m about to follow. The soundtrack that fits my mood is the latest album of Wilson Tanner. You might know one of the duo, under the name of Andras. Together the two Aussies create peaceful ambient, that makes you feel like being on a vineyard in rural Perth.

item.title: Amen Dunes - Freedom
item.description:
Today, on May 5th, we celebrate freedom in The Netherlands. Exactly 80 years ago the German occupation ended.

Last week in Scotland I was reminded of the country’s long fight for independence, when I learned about a statue of William Wallace from the movie Braveheart, as played by Mel Gibson, in the city of Stirling. The word ‘Freedom’ is written on the base of the statue, referring to the famous quote “they may take our lives, but they’ll never take our freedom”. Because the thing is pretty ugly, and has the face of Mel Gibson, the Scots ridiculed and vandalised it. To protect it, a fence was placed around it. The result: an encased Braveheart figure standing for freedom. Oh, the irony.

item.title: Letta Mbulu - In The Music The Village Never Ends
item.description: About ten years ago during Afro heyday, virtually every DJ in Amsterdam carried the down-tempo ‘Normalizo’ of this album. I heard it so often, I couldn’t listen to the South African Letta Mbulu for a long while. However, recently I started playing the album again because of the last track, ‘The Village’. It takes me back to a memorable moment at the end of a beautiful night in the basement of De School. At around 6 in the morning, after an hour of spacey twisted techno, this uplifting call-and-response tune woke me up and let me leave the club with a big smiling face.

item.title: Black Devil Disco Club - Black Devil Disco Club
item.description:
During Christmas, a dinner at a friend’s place ended in dancing in the kitchen and eventually moving to the club for a long night out. One thing that got us going was the record player in that kitchen and the extensive vinyl collection of the owner.

The record that did it for me, and which I played again during the hangover, was Black Devil Disco Club’s first release from 1978. This six-track EP is a contiguous trip down the depths of disco hell. You get taken along on a kick-snare ride with both refreshing and disturbing synthesizer noises and echoing sing-alongs. I was surprised to find out this record is from the 70’s, as many of the sounds can be still be heard in modern dance music today.

item.title: Discovery Zone - Remote Control
item.description: Do you remember the early days of the internet, when surfing the web sounded like visiting a parallel universe and AI was seen as something with supernatural powers? That’s the vibe I get from listening to JJ Weihl (New York) aka Discovery Zone. Last week I went to her concert in Cinetol, together with fellow Listenings writer Mark, and dear Listenings listener Isa. The setup was amazing, with Discovery Zone standing behind a see-through screen on which nostalgic cyberspace animations were beamed throughout the show. Imagine flying dolphins, geometrical pulsating patterns and lively color streams. A well designed mix between irony and beauty. The whole experience left me feeling excited for a time to come yet already passed.

item.title: John Maus - We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves
item.description:
Last week I went to Paradiso in Amsterdam to see John Maus for the first time. I had not listened to his music since the release of his album ‘We Must Become the Pitiless Censors of Ourselves’ in 2011, and I had no idea what to expect from the show.

When support act Pol finished and took their guitars, drums and synthesisers, all that was left was a laptop in the middle of the stage. Soon John walked up and kneeled in front of the computer, turning his back to the audience, and hit the play button. He then jumped up and went raving and running like a maniac across the stage, shouting into the microphone over the prerecorded music, inviting the audience to shout along. The scene reminded me of a pumped up priest spreading God’s energy in a church. This thing repeated every time he put on the next song, until he was soaking wet from sweat.

item.title: Don Ray - The Garden of Love
item.description: This is my go-to record pick when I’m home alone cooking, cleaning or dancing. It’s just sitting there with its bright coloured square letters, shouting to be pulled out of the cabinet. You might know the opening track Got to Have Loving, if not the original then maybe the highly sought-after edit by Oceanic, for which he took a sample from the amazing 2-minute break halfway the track. However, often I prefer to put the record on my turntable B-side up, starting with the the dripping arpeggio’s of Standing in the Rain, followed by the instant happiness of Garden of Love, ending with the slow but powerful My Desire.

item.title: Noami Sharon - Obsidian
item.description: Last weekend on Down The Rabbit Hole, I was eating very tasty fish and chips from Zijpe Stijl in between the performances from RAYE and Eefje de Visser. Once home, I realised that on that very moment, Naomi Sharon was playing on the other end of the festival. In the weeks before I had played her album Obsidian repeatedly, wanting to check her out. Oh well, that’s how it goes. I now like to assure myself that she probably didn’t match up to the shows of RAYE and Eefje anyway, which were amazing.

item.title: John Talabot - Fin
item.description:
Two weeks ago on Lentekabinet, I was somehow dissapointed to find out John Talabot had jumped on the trance train that has been riding for a bit too long. Along with DJ’s such as Job Jobse and Young Marco, Talabot is speeding way beyond the 130 limit.

I know I sound like a grumpy old man now…

Luckily, at home I can play the low BPMs of 2011’s release ‘Fin’. A true classic in it’s genre, according to many of my dancefloor friends. It takes me back to the days my feet could still meet the beat and makes me hopeful for a downtempo revival after the superfast music hype is over.

item.title: Various Artists – Heisei No Oto (Japanese Left-Field Pop From The CD Age, 1989-1996)
item.description:
In a few days I’ll be in Japan, together with fellow Listenings-writer Mark. I’m very excited to walk through the largest city on Earth, climb the 100,000 years old Mount Fuji and be surprised by a unique culture.

Evidently I’ve been listening to a lot of great Japanese music lately. The Heisei No Noto compilation by Music from Memory hits the spot for me. It contains many well composed dreamy ambient tracks, that take me to far away places yet to discover. There are also two more beat driven, almost Krautrocky, tunes I especially recommend you to listen to. Pi Po Pa by Yosui Inoue will probably unconsciously make you sing along to the three words of the title, leaving you with a feeling that everything will be alright. On Harai, Keisuke Sakurai sounds like the Japanese brother of Shaggy (you’re right Simon). Mr. Bombastic from Tokyo does a great job mumbling over a fine piano house beat.

item.title: The Boney King of Nowhere – Everybody Knows (2024)
item.description: When I ride my bicycle through the Utrechtsestraat in Amsterdam, I often make two stops. At the thrift shop in Kerkstraat, and at the second-hand house and techno bins of Concerto record store. There are always gems to be found in both places, which I perhaps should have kept to myself. Anyway, earlier this month I walked into Concerto and was greeted by the music the salesperson had put on. Moving on to the second-hand section, I turned around and asked at the counter if this was something by Radiohead that I did not know of. I have a group of friends who are die-hard Radiohead fans, and they will probably judge me for this, but I’m one of those listeners who structurally ignore a few of their albums.
